title: Postmortem: Prod Latency Spike - Zenith Health
summary: Review of 2025-04-08 production latency incident where certain inference requests experienced long tail p99 latency due to autoscaler thrash + KV cache warmup issues; discuss mitigations (fixed autoscaler window, prefix caching tweak, fallback model routing), initial timeline, and owner action items.
next_steps: Samira to share the postmortem doc and log extracts (link) by 2025-04-11
Diego to produce detailed GPU allocation + autoscaler timeline and telemetry by 2025-04-13
Schedule runbook workshop with Zenith SREs for 2025-04-17
action_items: Diego Ramos: produce timeline of GPU allocation, autoscaler events, and kernel selection logs; due 2025-04-13
Liu Chen: share SOC2/incident communication template and confirm audit log retention changes; due 2025-04-12
Priya Kapoor: provide exact list of customer routes affected and traffic samples; due 2025-04-11
Samira Patel: send postmortem doc, link to benchmark spreadsheet, and recommended config patch; due 2025-04-11
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-04-10 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Liu (Redwood CSM), Priya (Zenith SRE), Markus (Zenith Platform), Dana (Zenith CTO)
Artifacts referenced: postmortem draft (https://redwood.company/postmortems/zenith-2025-04-10), benchmark spreadsheet (https://sheets.redwood/zenith-bench), incident logs export (S3 link pasted in chat)

[00:00:05] Samira: hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have about 40 minutes. we'll walk through the timeline, what we think went wrong, and concrete mitigations. hi priya, can you kick us off with what you saw from your side?

[00:00:22] Priya: yeah thanks. so on 2025-04-08 around 02:13 UTC we saw a spike in p95/p99 latency for the inference route that handles clinical-summarization. latency rose from 120ms median to multiple seconds at p99, some requests timed out. it coincided with a deploy but initial look shows the new model was compatible. we saw autoscaler rapidly add and remove GPU nodes — kind of thrash — and the KV cache warmup seemed slow, so cold starts were expensive.

[00:00:47] Diego: okay, quick clarifying q — when you say autoscaler thrash, do you mean scale-up then immediate scale-down because of a short assessment window? or more of a provisioning/backpressure issue at the cloud provider?

[00:01:02] Markus: mostly scale up then within a minute scale down. our cloud team reported a few preemptible instances rebooting too which made the pool fluctuate. so yes both policy window and some infrastructure churn.

[00:01:20] Liu: i'll note we also saw a simultaneous increase in small bursty requests from one internal job that hit a few large prefix patterns, which exacerbated cache misses. so KV cache saw low hit-rate during the window.

[00:01:36] Dana: the real customer impact was timed-out clinical summaries during business hours in EU region — some downstream queues filled. we had to route traffic to a backup model but that impacted quality. not ideal.

[00:01:50] Samira: right. i pulled a preliminary timeline into the postmortem doc. (link in chat) the hypothesis we're leaning on is threefold: short autoscaler evaluation window + instance churn + cold KV cache on newly provisioned GPUs. that combination created long tail latency.

[00:02:10] Priya: can you expand on the KV cache part? we thought Redwood's prefix/KV cache should persist across pods for dedicated pools?

[00:02:22] Diego: yes good q. for dedicated pools we do persistent prefix caching when the same allocation serves repeated prefixes; however when instances are preempted or autoscaler rebalances, those caches are lost because the KV lives in local GPU memory plus ephemeral host. we do have options — we can enable a shared external KV (we call prefix-cache-backend) or tune our autoscaler to prefer draining before scale-down, or keep a small reserve pool to avoid immediate re-provisioning.

[00:02:55] Markus: what's the perf delta for shared external KV? i worry about added network hops and p99 impact.

[00:03:07] Diego: from our bench runs, shared KV adds about 8-15ms median but improves p99 dramatically if hit-rates are high because you avoid full model recompute. but the big win is avoiding the large 500ms+ cold-start cost for long sequences. there are tradeoffs. the bench sheet shows numbers per model and sequence length — link in chat.

[00:03:27] Priya: also want to flag security/compliance angle — the customer data is PHI for us, so any shared external cache must be encrypted and meet KMS controls. do you have KMS/HSM integrations for the cache store?

[00:03:41] Liu: yes we do. Redwood Private supports KMS integration and HSM-backed keys for vaulting cache encryption keys. for hosted we can enable envelope encryption tied to account KMS. we'll add exact config details to the postmortem.

[00:03:56] Dana: OK good. what about fallback model routing — you mentioned you routed to backup. how do we formalize that in a runbook?

[00:04:06] Samira: we recommend a two-tier fallback: first, automatic fallback to a compatible smaller model in the same family for latency spikes; second, route to an isolated, always-on reserve pool for critical routes. that reserve pool would be a small committed capacity to avoid 0->N provisioning.

[00:04:22] Priya: that's helpful. can you give an example config? like target 5% traffic to reserve pool or force fallback at x ms?

[00:04:33] Diego: example we use is: if p95 > 300ms for 2 continuous minutes, shift 30% of new requests to fallback tier for 10 minutes, and increase reserve nodes by one until p95 stabilizes. i'm paraphrasing but we'll paste the exact policy as a suggested patch.

[00:04:52] Markus: will that interact poorly with autoscaler? we don't want competing signals.

[00:04:58] Diego: good point. the policy should be outside of autoscaler's aggressive scale-down. autoscaler needs a slightly longer cool-down when fallback triggers, or the orchestration should be aware of fallback state and avoid scaling down reserve nodes.

[00:05:13] Priya: did logs show any model OOMs or kernel selection fallback?

[00:05:19] Diego: nothing obvious; kernel selection was stable but the big metric was the cache miss ratio and the time spent waiting on KV rehydration. we also saw queueing at the request dispatcher because the newly started GPU processes were still loading quantized weights.

[00:05:35] Liu: also FYI, the customer raised the question in the escalation: can Redwood provide an SLA credit for this outage window? i know that's a sales/legal conversation but wanted to flag.

[00:05:46] Samira: noted. we'll follow up with account and legal — for this call we're focused on tech mitigations, but i'll include the contact for our legal ops.

[00:05:56] Dana: timeline wise, what immediate mitigations can we push now?

[00:06:02] Diego: immediate ones: 1) increase autoscaler cool-down to 3-5 minutes, 2) enable a small reserve pool (1-2 GPUs) for the affected region, 3) enable prefix-cache-backend for the clinical-summarization route as an opt-in. those three reduce the chance of repeat. longer-term: move to shared encrypted KV in Private deployment or add checkpointed cache persistence across nodes.

[00:06:29] Priya: the enable cache backend — is that a config flag we can flip today or does it require code rollout?

[00:06:36] Diego: it's a config toggle for Dedicated/Hosted but we need to provision the external Redis/kv store and KMS keys; Redwood can provision or we can integrate with your existing managed Redis if you prefer. flipping the flag is low-risk but we should test in staging first.

[00:06:52] Markus: can we get an estimate for effort and risk?

[00:06:56] Diego: quick estimate: provision + test in staging ~1-2 days; enable in prod as opt-in ~1 day; monitor for 24-48 hours. engineering risk is low if we use an isolated namespace and enforce encryption.

[00:07:10] Priya: on the monitoring side, what new alerts should we add?

[00:07:14] Liu: suggested alerts: sustained p95 > threshold for 2 mins, autoscaler scale events > x per hour (detect thrash), cache hit-rate below y% for critical routes, and provisioning failure rates. we'll provide the exact alert rules.

[00:07:29] Priya: perfect. also, for compliance, can you include an audit log snippet showing who changed configs and when? we got asked by internal auditors during the incident.

[00:07:38] Diego: yes we have config audit trails in the console; we'll include a sanitized snippet in the postmortem.

[00:07:45] Dana: what about cost impact for reserve pool? i need a ballpark for execs.

[00:07:51] Samira: for a small reserve pool of 2 x A10-like GPUs, ballpark is $X/day — we'll compute exact numbers based on your committed discount. Diego will include a token-level cost delta in the follow-up.

[00:08:04] Markus: one more question — during the spike, did we see any request-level token accounting anomalies? i.e., were costs mis-attributed?

[00:08:12] Diego: no anomalies in token accounting; the billing events trace to the correct model id and route. there was some delayed reporting in analytics pipeline but billing is intact.

[00:08:22] Priya: ok. let's talk timeline: we want the following in the next week: postmortem doc, autoscaler config change, staging test of prefix-cache-backend, and runbook workshop. are those feasible?

[00:08:36] Samira: yes. we'll aim to deliver docs and autoscaler patch by 2025-04-11, Diego will own staging test by 2025-04-13, and we'll set the runbook workshop for 2025-04-17 as suggested.

[00:08:47] Dana: thanks. also want to request a short external-facing summary we can send to our stakeholders — minimal technical detail but impact and remediation.

[00:08:56] Liu: we can draft a one-page customer-facing summary and send to Priya + Dana for signoff before you circulate.

[00:09:03] Samira: great. any other technical outstanding q's?

[00:09:08] Markus: small one — you mentioned quantization/weights loading contributing to startup delays. is there a quick win like checkpointed weights on disk to speed startup?

[00:09:18] Diego: yes two small wins: 1) use memory-mapped weight files (mmapped) so the process start touches less memory before tokens arrive, 2) pre-warm the model on reserve nodes. mmapping is low-effort but still needs a controlled rollout. we'll include that in the tech checklist.

[00:09:34] Priya: fantastic. thanks all — we'll expect the doc and timeline.

[00:09:39] Samira: recap — Samira to share postmortem and links by EOD 2025-04-11; Diego to produce detailed autoscaler + GPU timeline and run staging test; Liu to send the external one-page summary and audit log snippet; Priya to share affected routes and traffic samples. Schedule runbook workshop for 2025-04-17.

[00:09:59] Dana: sounds good. we'll loop in procurement/legal for SLA/credits separately.

[00:10:07] Samira: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with action items and calendar invites. ending call.

End of transcript.
